title: Angle and Grid Finder
context: Grade 4, the closing topic, which gathers two sections the page runs together. An adult sees angles and a grid of pictures. What is actually being settled is two ways of saying exactly where something is. For angles, the page gives obtuse no upper limit, and clock hands always make two angles at once, so this tool always names the smaller one. For the grid, the page's section is headed MAP and promises position, direction and distance, but it never shows a map; what it shows is a grid read by rows and columns, and the one sentence that uses them says the pomegranate is three columns below the strawberry, when the two are three rows apart in one column. This tool teaches position on a grid by row and column, and nothing a map would add.

writeup.why: Name an angle and sort it against a square corner, read the smaller angle between clock hands, and find a place on a grid by its row and its column.
writeup.look: Hinged arms and a clock face on the left of the canvas, a square-corner card between them, and a grid of pictures with numbered rows and columns on the right.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Angle and Grid Finder' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the names built, the angles sorted or the moves made against what this phase asks for, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each name settles, each kind lands or each move is made, and the second fixed at what this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The working area is split in two. On the left, two deep blue arms are hinged at a point, 330 by 290 at 64,214, each arm draggable to open or close the angle between them, with a capital letter at the end of each arm and a vermilion dot and letter at the point where they meet, and an amber arc drawn between the arms close to that point, or a square corner mark when the angle is a right angle. The name builder runs under the arms, 330 by 56 at 64,516, writing the angle's name as its letters are tapped and settling it only with the meeting letter in the middle. The square-corner card rests at 410,214, 120 by 120, a paper corner with its square corner mark in amber, and can be dragged into any angle with one edge along an arm: it fits exactly, or the second arm lies inside it, or a space is left between it and the second arm, lit. The clock face stands under the card, 220 across at 400,346, with an hour hand and a longer minute hand that snap to point exactly at the numbers; both angles between the hands are shaded at once, the larger in sky blue, and the smaller is outlined. The hour counter sits under the clock, 220 by 56 at 400,582, and steps round the gaps between the numbers from one hand to the other, each way round in turn, counting the hours apart and never the numbers passed. On the right the picture grid stands 480 by 480 at 660,226: four rows and four columns of cells 110 on a side, holding sixteen different pictures with no picture appearing twice, the row numbers in a strip 40 wide down its left edge, counted from the top, and the column numbers in a strip 40 tall across its top, counted from the left. The marker is a ring round one cell and moves one step at a time, down or up by rows and across by columns; as it moves, its whole row lights across the grid and its whole column lights down it, and the row and column numbers at the edges light with them. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is a word pad wherever a kind or a name is asked for, with keys reading right angle, acute and obtuse and the capital letters of the figure, and twelve number keys three across wherever a row, a column or a count of hours is asked for. The list of ten can do statements and the word pad of the chapter's twenty vocabulary words sit under the slot for the closing pages. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The figure being studied, every line, segment, ray, side, outline, circle, angle arm and visible edge of a solid, is deep blue. Every point, end point, corner dot, vertex dot and the centre dot of a circle is vermilion. A length being measured, walked, added or named, and every angle arc and square corner mark, is amber. The unit squares that cover an area, the flood inside a closed figure and a face of a solid being counted are green. A line of symmetry or a mirror line is reddish purple and always dotted. The second thing set beside the first, a fold being tried, a mirror image, the other half of a fold, a chord that is not a diameter and the larger angle between clock hands, is sky blue. A hidden edge of a solid is grey and dashed, and grey is used for nothing else. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every grid line, ruler tick, bracket, guide line and table rule is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a point is a round dot, a line carries an arrowhead at each end, a ray a dot and one arrowhead and a segment a dot at each end, a measured length carries its number, a hidden edge is dashed and a line of symmetry is dotted, before any of them is told by a colour. A dotted line always means a true line of symmetry or a mirror line, and a fold being tried is drawn solid until it is kept, so nothing else on any stage of this chapter is ever dotted. A clock here is never set to six o'clock or twelve o'clock, so its two angles are never equal and the smaller is always plain to see, and an angle between the hands is counted in hours apart against the three hours of a right angle. Every picture on the grid appears once, so a picture is found by its row and its column, and a miscount cannot land on the same picture somewhere else.
writeup.finish: The card shows the angles the child named and sorted, the clock with its smaller angle outlined, and the grid with the path the marker took.

phases.win: the name settles with the meeting letter in the middle and both arms lit from it
phases.does: opens the arms, names the arms and the vertex, and builds the angle's name
phases.goal: an angle is two arms from one vertex, named with the vertex in the middle
phases.says: Where do the two arms meet? Put that letter in the middle of the name.
phases.check: Draw an angle with its vertex at P and its arms through Q and R. Write three names for it.
phases.feels: the letter where the arms meet sits in the middle of a three-letter name, or stands alone
phases.hands: Hinge two pencils together at one end with a rubber band and open them. Ask where the two meet. Call that point the vertex, the corner the angle opens from, and call the pencils its arms. Letter the tip of each pencil and the vertex on sticky notes, and read the angle's name aloud with the vertex in the middle.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which point do both arms start from? Second rung, the phase's: where does that letter go in the name? Third rung: the arms are cut back so only the three letters show, and the name is built one letter at a time. The word pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: a name is read from the left, and the point that matters most seems to belong at the front.
wrong.move: names the angle with the vertex first, writing angle BAC for the angle at B.
wrong.screen: the name builder draws the angle the child's name describes, with its corner at A and its arms running to B and to C, shaded sky blue beside the angle at B, a different corner. The builder then writes the name with the meeting letter in the middle, and both names stay in the slot.

wrong.why: every point on the figure has a letter, and nothing about the letters says which one is the corner.
wrong.move: takes the point at the end of one arm for the vertex, because it carries a letter like the rest.
wrong.screen: the arms are traced from the child's point, and only one arm runs from it; from the meeting point both arms run out, and they light from there together. The meeting point takes its vermilion dot with the word vertex beside it, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: two hinged arms with a letter at each end and at the point where they meet
phases.soWhat: An angle is two arms from one vertex, the corner where they meet, and it is named with the vertex in the middle or by the vertex alone.

phases.win: the card settles in the angle and its kind lands beside it: right, acute or obtuse
phases.does: lays the card into the angle, reads how it fits, and sorts the angle
phases.goal: a right angle is a square corner, an acute angle is smaller and an obtuse angle is larger
phases.says: Lay the square corner in. Does it fit, cover an arm, or leave a space?
phases.check: Find one right angle, one acute angle and one obtuse angle in the room. Test each with a folded paper corner.
phases.feels: the square corner is the ruler for angles: it fits, it holds the arms inside, or it leaves a space
phases.hands: Fold a sheet of paper in half and in half again to make a square corner. Use it to test corners round the room: the corner of a desk, a door standing half open, a pair of open scissors and a book standing wide open. Sort each one as fits exactly, sits inside the paper corner, or leaves a space.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what does the square corner do when it is laid in? Second rung, the phase's: is the angle smaller or larger than the square corner? Third rung: the arms are set to a square corner first and then opened or closed a step at a time, with the card laid in at each step. The word pad stays open.

wrong.why: acute sounds like sharp and small, and a drawing with short arms looks small whatever its opening.
wrong.move: calls an angle bigger than a right angle acute, because it is drawn small or its arms are short.
wrong.screen: the square-corner card is laid into the angle with one edge along an arm, and a space opens between the card's other edge and the second arm, lit. The kind lands beside the angle as obtuse, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: long arms take up a lot of the page, and a big drawing looks like a big angle.
wrong.move: calls a narrow angle obtuse because its arms are drawn long.
wrong.screen: the arms are made longer and then shorter while the opening between them stays exactly the same, and the card sits over the angle each time with both arms inside its edges. The kind stays acute throughout, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: the hinged arms opened to an angle, with the square-corner card beside them
phases.soWhat: A right angle is a square corner; an angle smaller than it is acute, and one larger than it is obtuse.

phases.win: the smaller angle is outlined, the square-corner card is laid against it, and its kind lands
phases.does: counts the hours between the hands each way round, picks the smaller angle, and sorts it
phases.goal: clock hands make two angles, and the one to name is the smaller
phases.says: The hands make two angles. Which is the smaller one? What kind is it?
phases.check: Set a paper clock to eight o'clock. Count the hours between the hands both ways. Name the smaller angle's kind.
phases.feels: the hands always make two angles, and the one to name is the gap between them the short way round
phases.hands: Hold up a paper clock with card hands set to three o'clock. Lay the folded paper corner between the hands: it fits. Count the gaps between the numbers from one hand to the other, three hours, and call that the square corner. Then set ten o'clock and ask the class to count the hours between the hands both ways round, and to name the smaller.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many hours apart are the hands the short way round? Second rung, the phase's: how many hours make a square corner? Third rung: the clock is set to three o'clock first and the card laid in, before the hour in the question comes back. The word pad stays open.

wrong.why: the page calls any angle bigger than a right angle obtuse, with no upper limit, and the hands do make a big angle the other way round.
wrong.move: names the larger angle, counting the long way round, and calls the angle at ten o'clock obtuse.
wrong.screen: both angles between the hands are shaded, the larger in sky blue, and the hours are counted round each way, ten one way and two the other. The smaller angle is outlined and the square-corner card is laid against it: its three hours reach past the two, so the angle sits inside the card. The child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: counting the numbers feels like counting the hours, and the number at each hand gets counted as well.
wrong.move: counts the numbers the angle covers instead of the gaps between them, making two o'clock three hours wide and so a right angle.
wrong.screen: the hour counter steps the gaps one at a time from one hand to the other, twelve to one and one to two, lighting each gap, and stops at two. The square-corner card is laid from the minute hand and reaches past the hour hand to three, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a clock face with its hands set to an hour and both angles shaded
phases.soWhat: Clock hands make two angles, and the one to name is the smaller: one or two hours apart is acute, three is a right angle, and four or five is obtuse.

phases.win: the marker lands, its row lights across and its column lights down, and the picture it sits on is named
phases.does: moves the marker by rows and columns as told and names the picture it reaches
phases.goal: a place on a grid is given by its row and its column, and moving down changes the row
phases.says: Move down. Which number changed, the row or the column?
phases.check: On a grid with rows counted from the top, start in row one, column four. Move three places straight down. Where are you now?
phases.feels: moving down, the row number changes and the column number stays, and moving across it is the other way round
phases.hands: Draw a grid of four rows and four columns on the board with a different picture in every cell, rows numbered down the left from the top and columns across the top from the left. Ask for the picture in row three, column two. Then move a paper marker two places straight down and ask which number changed, the row or the column.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which end is row one counted from on this grid? Second rung, the phase's: does this move go down or across? Third rung: the grid is cut to two rows and two columns, and the marker makes one move with its row and column lit before the larger grid comes back. The number pad and the word pad stay open.

wrong.why: the chapter's own sentence about the fruit grid names columns for a move straight down, when the two fruits it compares share a column, three rows apart.
wrong.move: calls a move straight down a move of so many columns, though the column never changes.
wrong.screen: the marker is moved down one step at a time from its start, and at each step a new row lights across the grid while its column stays lit down it, unchanged. The row number at the left edge climbs by one at each step, the column number at the top stays the same, and the child's answer stays in the slot beside them.

wrong.why: on the page's own fruit grid the same fruit sits three times, once in the very row asked about, so a child who miscounts the columns still names the fruit that is asked for and is told so.
wrong.move: names the picture that looks right at a glance without counting its row and column, so a miscount can still land on the right name.
wrong.screen: the marker is set on the child's picture where it sits, and its row and column light at the edges beside the row and column the question gave; where they differ, both cells ring. The slot then asks for the row and the column as well as the picture, so an answer names the place and not only the thing.

phases.screen: the picture grid with its rows numbered down the left and its columns across the top, and the marker at a start
phases.soWhat: A place on a grid is given by its row and its column. Rows run across and columns run down, so moving down changes the row and keeps the column.

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, the moment the marker moves straight down. Its whole row slides down with it, lighting a fresh line of pictures across the grid, while the lit column it travels along stays exactly where it was, and the row number at the left edge ticks on by one at each step with the column number at the top never changing. Move it across and the opposite happens. It can be walked round the grid as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase two arms stand hinged at a point on the left of the working area, a capital letter at the end of each arm and at the point where they meet, with the name builder empty under them. On the second the arms stand opened to an angle with the square-corner card lying beside them. On the third the clock face stands with its hands set to an hour, both angles between them shaded and neither outlined. On the fourth the picture grid stands on the right, its rows numbered down its left edge from the top and its columns across its top from the left, with the marker ringing one cell. The running count at the top left holds the names built, the angles sorted or the moves made against what this phase asks for, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the meeting point, or the square-corner card, or the hour counter, or the marker, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks where the two arms meet. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any angle on the hinged arms, any hour on the clock, and any move on the grid, with the square-corner card and the row and column lights open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on naming angles, sorting them against a square corner, the smaller angle between clock hands, and places and moves on a grid.
voiceLines: Two arms from one point, a clock and a grid. Where do the two arms meet?
Where do the two arms meet? Put that letter in the middle of the name.
Lay the square corner in. Does it fit, cover an arm, or leave a space?
The hands make two angles. Which is the smaller one? What kind is it?
Move down. Which number changed, the row or the column?
A new one. Find the vertex, or row one, before anything moves.
Free play. Any angle, any hour, any move on the grid, with the square corner open.
Lay the square corner in again, count the hours again, or walk the marker one step at a time.
Every angle named from its vertex, every clock read the short way round, and every move told by row and column.

observations.why: The middle letter says where the angle opens from, and the other two only say which way its arms point.
observations.soWhat: Name an angle with its vertex, the corner, in the middle, or by the vertex alone.
observations.observe: The name settled only with the meeting letter in the middle.

observations.why: A right angle is a square corner, and every other angle is smaller or larger than it.
observations.soWhat: An acute angle is smaller than a right angle and an obtuse angle is larger, however long the arms are drawn.
observations.observe: The square-corner card fitted, held the arms inside it, or left a space, and that sorted every angle.

observations.why: The hands split the clock face into two gaps, one each way round.
observations.soWhat: Name the smaller angle between clock hands, counted in hours apart against the three hours of a right angle.
observations.observe: At every hour the hands made two angles, and only the smaller was outlined.

observations.why: Rows run across the grid and columns run down it.
observations.soWhat: Moving down or up changes the row and keeps the column, and moving across changes the column and keeps the row.
observations.observe: A move down lit a new row across the grid and kept the same column lit.

source_tool.description: On the left of the stage two arms are hinged at a point, and dragging either arm opens or closes the angle between them; a letter sits at the end of each arm and at the point where they meet, and the angle's name is built with the meeting letter in the middle. A square-corner card can be laid into any angle: if it fits exactly the angle is a right angle, if the arms sit inside it the angle is acute, and if a space is left between the card and an arm the angle is obtuse. A clock face beside it has an hour hand and a longer minute hand that point exactly at the numbers. The two angles the hands make are shaded at once, the smaller one is outlined, and the hours between the hands are counted round each way, so the smaller angle can be laid against the square corner that three hours make. On the right, a grid of pictures carries its row numbers down the left edge and its column numbers across the top, with every picture appearing once. A marker moves by rows down or up and by columns across, and as it moves its whole row lights across the grid and its whole column lights down it, so a move down is seen to change the row and keep the column.
source_tool.art_direction: Hinged arms, a clock and a grid / Picture book

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a drawing board with a ruler and a point stamp, a tracing finger and a flag, a walker and a string, square tiles on squared paper, a pair of compasses with a metal point and a pencil arm, a sheet of paper that folds, an upright mirror, solids on a turntable, flat nets that fold up, hinged arms, a clock face and a grid of pictures.

A line is always drawn with an arrowhead at each end, a ray with a dot at its end point and one arrowhead, and a line segment with a dot at each end. No stroke is ever left with a bare end that could be read as either.

A point is drawn as one small dot of one size wherever it appears, named by a capital letter beside it. Within one figure no letter ever names two different things, and a figure never renames a part it has already named.

Every labelled length is one the figure could really have, and every figure is drawn to scale with its labels. A triangle drawn with a square corner carries lengths such as three, four and five, and a stepped shape's sides close up exactly.
A figure on squared paper sits exactly on the grid lines, with every side along a line and every square either wholly inside it or wholly outside it.

A circle drawn to show its parts has its centre marked as a dot and named. Every radius is drawn from that dot to the curve, and a diameter always passes exactly through the dot. A circle that is a view of a solid carries a dot only where the solid has a point, so a cylinder seen from above is a plain circle.
A right angle carries a small square corner mark, and every other angle an arc drawn close to its vertex between the arms.

A line of symmetry and a mirror line are drawn dotted and lie exactly where the fold falls. A fold line being tried is drawn solid and turns dotted only once the fold is kept. Every mirror line stands upright unless the frame says it lies across, and an image sits exactly as far behind the line as the thing in front of it, turned the other way round.
A solid is drawn with its hidden edges dashed. Views of one solid are drawn at one scale, so the front view and the side view of a box are exactly the same height.

Clock hands point exactly at the numbers and the minute hand is the longer. Where the angle between the hands is shown, both angles are shaded and the smaller one is outlined. No clock is set to six o'clock or twelve o'clock.
A grid carries its row numbers down the left edge and its column numbers across the top, and each picture in it appears once.
A shape, a side or a part is told apart by its label first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a line, a point, a square or a part the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The figure being studied, every line, segment, ray, side, outline, circle, angle arm and visible edge of a solid, is deep blue. Every point, end point, corner dot, vertex dot and the centre dot of a circle is vermilion, in every tool without exception, because a chapter that opens on the point cannot afford a frame where a point has to be hunted for. A length being measured, walked, added or named, the tape, the walker's sum, a radius being measured, and every angle arc and square corner mark, is amber. The unit squares that cover an area, the flood inside a closed figure and a face of a solid being counted are green. A line of symmetry or a mirror line is reddish purple and always dotted, so a dotted line always means a true line of symmetry. Sky blue is the second thing set beside the first: a fold being tried, drawn solid until it is kept, a mirror image, the other half of a fold, a chord that is not a diameter, and the larger angle between clock hands. A hidden edge of a solid is grey and dashed, and grey is used for nothing else. Every grid line, ruler tick, bracket, guide line and table rule is near-black chrome. All of that holds in greyscale, because a point is a round dot, a measured length carries its number, a line of symmetry is dotted, a fold being tried is solid and a hidden edge is dashed.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Lay the square corner in again, count the hours again, or walk the marker one step at a time.
voice.onNext: A new one. Find the vertex, or row one, before anything moves.
voice.opening: Two arms from one point, a clock and a grid. Where do the two arms meet?
voice.onFinish: Every angle named from its vertex, every clock read the short way round, and every move told by row and column.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any angle, any hour, any move on the grid, with the square corner open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has walked to desks named by a row and a column, and before any clock or grid on the page is read. The tool is what shades both angles between the hands at once and lights a whole row and a whole column as a marker moves, which a printed clock and a printed grid cannot do.

answer_key.rule: An angle is formed where two rays meet. The rays are its arms and the point they share is its vertex, and the angle is named by three letters with the vertex in the middle, or by the vertex alone. A right angle is a square corner. An angle smaller than a right angle is acute, and one larger than a right angle is obtuse. Clock hands make two angles at once, and the one to name is the smaller: at three o'clock and at nine o'clock it is a right angle, when the hands are fewer than three hours apart it is acute, and when they are four or five hours apart it is obtuse. A place on a grid is given by its row and its column. Rows run across and columns run down, so moving down or up changes the row and keeps the column, and moving across changes the column and keeps the row.
answer_key.wrong: The square-corner card is laid in the angle again and the hours are counted round each way aloud, and on the grid the marker goes back to its start and moves again one step at a time with its row and column lit. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The two rays share the point B, so B is where the arms meet.
The arms are the rays BA and BC, each starting at B.
The angle is named with the vertex in the middle, angle ABC or angle CBA, or by the vertex alone, angle B.
items.answer: Angle ABC, which is also angle CBA or angle B. Its arms are rays BA and BC, and its vertex is B
items.question: Rays BA and BC start from point B. Name the angle they make, its arms and its vertex.
items.checkpoint: An angle has two arms and a vertex, and its name has the vertex in the middle.
items.misconception: Naming it angle BAC, with the vertex first, which names a different angle.

steps: The corner of a page is a square corner, which is a right angle.
The first angle fits it exactly, so it is a right angle too.
The second is smaller than the square corner, so it is an acute angle.
items.answer: The first is a right angle, and the second is acute
items.question: The corner of a page fits exactly into one angle. A second angle is so narrow that its arms sit inside the page's corner. What kinds of angle are they?
items.checkpoint: A right angle is a square corner; a smaller angle is acute, and a larger one is obtuse.
items.misconception: Calling a narrow angle obtuse because its arms are drawn long.

steps: At ten o'clock the minute hand points at twelve and the hour hand at ten.
Counting one way round they are ten hours apart, and the other way only two.
Name the smaller angle: two hours is less than the three hours that make a square corner, so it is acute.
items.answer: Acute. The smaller angle between the hands is two hours wide, less than the three hours of a right angle
items.question: At ten o'clock, what kind of angle do the hands of a clock make?
items.checkpoint: Clock hands make two angles, and the one to name is the smaller.
items.misconception: Counting from twelve round to ten, finding ten hours, and calling the angle obtuse.

steps: Moving across to the right changes the column: from column one, two across is column three, still in row one.
Moving down changes the row: from row one, three down is row four, still in column three.
So the marker stops in row four, column three.
items.question: On a grid, rows are counted from the top and columns from the left. A marker starts in row one, column one. It moves two columns across to the right, then three rows down. Where does it stop?
items.checkpoint: Moving across changes the column, and moving down changes the row.
items.misconception: Counting the starting square as the first step, or moving down by columns, and landing in the wrong place.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: An angle is named angle DEF. Which letter is its vertex, and which rays are its arms?
items.final_answer: E is the vertex, and the arms are rays ED and EF

items.question: Rays OS and OT start from point O. Give three names for the angle they make.
items.final_answer: Angle SOT, angle TOS and angle O

items.question: The blades of a pair of scissors open to an angle smaller than the corner of a page. What kind of angle is it?
items.final_answer: Acute, because it is smaller than a right angle

items.question: A book stands open with its covers wider apart than a square corner. What kind of angle do the covers make?
items.final_answer: Obtuse. A square-corner card laid in the angle leaves a space between itself and one cover

items.question: What kind of angle do the hands of a clock make at four o'clock?
items.final_answer: Obtuse. The smaller angle is four hours wide, more than the three hours of a right angle

items.question: At nine o'clock, the hands are three hours apart one way and nine hours apart the other. Which angle do you name, and what kind is it?
items.final_answer: The smaller one, three hours wide, which is a right angle

items.question: A grid has rows counted from the top. Row one: bell, kite, drum, boat. Row two: star, cup, lamp, tent. Row three: ball, fish, leaf, sock. Start at the kite and move two rows down. Which picture do you reach?
items.final_answer: The fish, in row three, column two, the same column as the kite

items.question: In a grid with rows counted from the top, a drum is in row one, column three, and a leaf is in row three, column three. A child says the leaf is two columns below the drum. What should the child say?
items.final_answer: The leaf is two rows below the drum, in the same column. Moving down changes the row, not the column

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: open and close an angle by dragging either arm
builds the angle's name with the meeting letter in the middle
lays a right angle into any angle to compare
set the hour and minute hands to point at the numbers
shades both angles between the hands and outlines the smaller
counts the hours between the hands each way round
moves by rows down or up and by columns across
light the marker's whole row across and whole column down

teaching_notes: Make a square corner by folding a sheet of paper in half and then in half again, and use it to sort every angle in the room before the tool is opened. An angle smaller than it is acute and one larger is obtuse. The page gives obtuse no upper limit, and clock hands always make two angles, so a child who counts round the long way at ten o'clock will call a narrow angle obtuse. Always name the smaller angle between the hands, and lay the paper corner against it. The page heads the next section MAP and never shows one. It shows a grid of fruit read by rows and columns, and then says the pomegranate is three columns below the strawberry; the two are in the same column, three rows apart. Say rows every time a move goes down. The grid's model question can also be answered right by a child who miscounts, because the same fruit sits twice in that row, so every grid here holds each picture once. Do not add directions, distances or scales the page never teaches. The chessboard in the last exercise counts its rows up from the bottom, so say which end row one is before any move is made.
generation_prompt: Build an angle and grid tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage, with the working area split in two. On the left, two arms are hinged at a point, each arm draggable to open or close the angle, with a capital letter at the end of each arm and at the meeting point, and a name builder writes the angle's name with the meeting letter in the middle. A square-corner card can be dragged into the angle; it shows the angle as right when it fits exactly, acute when the arms sit inside it, and obtuse when a space is left between the card and an arm. Beside it a clock face has an hour hand and a longer minute hand that snap to point exactly at the numbers, never set to six o'clock or twelve o'clock; both angles between the hands are shaded at once, the smaller is outlined, and the hours between the hands are counted round each way. On the right, a grid of four rows and four columns holds sixteen different pictures, with row numbers down the left edge and column numbers across the top. A marker moves one step at a time by rows down or up and by columns across; its whole row lights across the grid and its whole column lights down it as it moves. A list of ten can do statements and a word pad of the chapter's twenty vocabulary words sit under the slot. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Name an angle with the meeting point in the middle. Lay the square corner in to sort it. On a clock, name the smaller angle. On the grid, moving down changes the row. Moving across changes the column.
